title: The Good News and the World's Guilt
sum: Paul introduces himself to a church he has never visited, in one long sentence (1:1–7) that names his message and his task. The message is the good news God promised in the Scriptures about his Son, a descendant of David, marked out as Son of God with power by his resurrection. The task is to bring the Gentiles to "the obedience of faith." He thanks God for the Romans' reputation, tells them he has often tried to visit, and says he is eager to preach in Rome too (1:8–15).

Then comes the thesis of the whole letter (1:16–17): the good news is God's power to save everyone who believes, Jew first and also Greek, because in it God's righteousness is revealed, as Habakkuk said. The rest of the chapter (1:18–32) begins the long argument that all humanity needs it: God's anger is revealed against people who held down the truth about him, swapped his glory for images, and were handed over to what they chose. The passage reads like a Jewish sermon against pagans, and it sets a trap that closes in 2:1.
readings: Read as a sermon against the nations

The traditional reading takes 1:18–32 as the standard Jewish case against Gentile idolatry and vice, like Wisdom of Solomon 13–14 (a book that is Scripture for Catholic and Orthodox Christians). Paul's Jewish readers would nod along. The point of the paragraph is that the world needs the good news, and it has no excuse.
Read as the story of Adam and Israel

Another reading hears Genesis behind the verses: a humanity that knew God, refused thanks, and was driven from the garden of knowledge into confusion (Hooker, Wright). The echoes of Psalm 106:20 and Jeremiah 2:11 suggest that Israel's golden calf is in the picture as well (Hays). On this reading "they" is everyone, Israel included.
Read as the first move in a trap

A third reading sees the paragraph as a rhetorical setup: Paul describes the sins of the nations in terms any moralist, Jew or Gentile, will applaud, so that 2:1 can turn on the reader (Stowers; also Hays and many commentators in part). The passage then is not mainly a statement about sexual ethics or about the pagan world but a step in an argument about everyone.

views.H: Paul writes from Corinth in the winter of about AD 56–57 (some date it a year earlier or later) to house churches in a city of perhaps a million people, with synagogues, a Jewish community that had been expelled by Claudius about AD 49 (Suetonius, Claudius 25.4; Acts 18:2) and was returning after 54. The empire called its rulers' announcements "good news" (the Priene inscription of 9 BC), and Paul claims the word for a different king.
views.C: Authorship is not in doubt: Romans is undisputedly Paul's, written down by a scribe named Tertius (16:22). Debate centers on why he wrote it (the "Romans debate," see the introduction) and on small textual questions at once: "in Rome" is missing from a few manuscripts at 1:7 and 1:15; the Byzantine text adds "of Christ" at 1:16. 1:3–4 is widely thought to quote an earlier creed.
views.L: The opening sentence is the longest of Paul's greetings. 1:5 and 16:26 frame the letter with "the obedience of faith." 1:16–17 is the thesis, built on Habakkuk 2:4, and 1:18 begins to prove it. The style turns from letter to lecture at 1:18 and becomes a diatribe at 2:1. The pivot word is "handed over" (1:24, 26, 28), which comes back at 4:25 and 8:32.
views.J: Paul calls himself a slave of the Messiah and an apostle, but the language of 1:1–7 is Jewish through and through: the prophets, the Scriptures, David's line. "The Jew first" is not a ranking but an order. The attack on idolatry and the list of vices belong to a Jewish tradition of polemic against pagans (Wisdom of Solomon 13–14; Philo; Josephus). Jewish scholars have noted how Paul's argument depends on his readers' sharing that tradition (Levine, Jewish Annotated New Testament; Fredriksen).
views.T: Origen's commentary (in Rufinus' Latin) and Chrysostom's homilies read 1:19–20 as proof that creation teaches God, and 1:24–28 as God's judgment in letting sin run. Augustine's early readings of 1:17 gave way to his later teaching on grace. Luther's preface (1522) calls Romans "the chief part of the New Testament and the purest gospel." Calvin opened his commentary by saying that whoever understands Romans has a way into all of Scripture. For Catholic teaching since Vatican I, 1:20 is the text on the natural knowledge of God.

deep.b:
These two verses say what the rest of the letter will prove. (1) The good news is not just words: it is God's power for salvation. (2) It is for everyone who believes, the Jew first and the Greek as well. (3) In it God's righteousness is revealed "from faith to faith." (4) The proof is Habakkuk 2:4.

Each phrase is disputed, and the notes set out the readings: whether "God's righteousness" is a gift, God's justice, his faithfulness to his covenant or his saving power; whether "from faith to faith" describes growth, stages or only emphasis; and whether Habakkuk's "the righteous will live by faith" means that the person who is righteous by faith will live, or that the righteous will live by faith. The Qumran commentary on Habakkuk (1QpHab 8) and the Talmud (Makkot 24a) both treat the verse as the center of the Torah.

Three times Paul says that God "handed them over" (1:24, 26, 28). The verb is the verb of a court: a prisoner is handed over. Paul does not say that God makes people sin. He says that God lets human choices run to their end, and that this letting-go is itself the form God's anger takes now (1:18).

The verb returns with a different meaning: Jesus "was handed over for our trespasses" (4:25), and God did not spare his own Son but handed him over for us all (8:32). Readers who follow the word see a pattern: the Son is handed over into the place where humanity was handed over. Commentators have noticed the repeated verb; it is hard to miss in the Greek.

deep.title: Claude's theory: three exchanges, three hand-overs, three scenes
deep.b:
1:22–32 has three "exchange" sentences, each followed by a hand-over. Humans swap God's glory for images (1:23) and God hands them over to impurity (1:24). They swap the truth for the lie (1:25) and God hands them over to shameful passions (1:26). They refuse to keep God in their knowledge (1:28) and God hands them over to a mind that fails the test, so that they do what is not fitting (1:28–31). The movement is from worship, to the body, to the community.

My suggestion is that the three steps follow the order of the Ten Words: first God, then the family, then the neighbors. The idol is the first table; sex and honor are the family; and the list of vices (envy, murder, strife, deceit, disobedience to parents) reads like the second table. This is a pattern, not a proof; Paul does not point it out. It overlaps with the Wisdom of Solomon (Scripture for Catholic and Orthodox Christians), which also runs from idols to sexual sin to social vice (Wisdom of Solomon 14:12, 22–27), and with Richard Hays and others who find the Genesis story behind 1:18–32. The reading would tie 1:18–32 to 2:21–22, where Paul quotes the commandments by name.
deep.refs: Wisdom of Solomon 14:12; Wisdom of Solomon 14:22–27; Exodus 20:1–17; Romans 2:21–22

echoes: Habakkuk 2:4; Psalm 19:1–4; Psalm 106:20; Jeremiah 2:11; Isaiah 52:7; Genesis 1–3; Wisdom of Solomon 13–14; Leviticus 18:22; Leviticus 20:13; Acts 14:15–17; Acts 17:22–31; Galatians 1:11–17; Hebrews 10:38

settings.to: All of God's loved ones in Rome who are called to be saints: Jewish and Gentile believers who met in several house gatherings and had never been visited by Paul
settings.when: Winter of about AD 56–57, from Corinth, just before Paul takes the collection to Jerusalem
settings.why: To introduce himself to a church he did not found, to name his authority as a slave of Christ and an apostle, and to state in a creed-like sentence the good news he and they hold in common (1:3–4). He says plainly that his calling is to the Gentiles (1:5–6, 13), which prepares for his claim to speak to them.
settings.readers: Believers in the capital, probably including Jewish Christians who had returned after the edict of Claudius had lapsed, and Gentile Christians who, on one common reconstruction (Wedderburn, Lampe), had led the house churches in their absence. The mix, and the tension between them, is on that view the likely reason for much of the letter.
views: Paul's words in 1:5–6 and 1:13 and his address to "you Gentiles" (11:13) suggest that most of the readers were Gentiles, with a Jewish minority (Moo, Fitzmyer).
A mixed church with Jewish leadership
The arguments about the law, circumcision and Abraham suggest a strongly Jewish-Christian setting, or that the Gentile Christians had learned their faith from Jewish teachers (Dunn, Wright).

settings.when: At the opening of a letter, as Greek letters began with thanks to the gods
settings.why: To win their goodwill, to explain why he has not yet come (he has been hindered; his mission lay elsewhere, 15:22–23), and to say that he is eager to preach to them as well. It prepares for his request for help with the mission to Spain (15:24).
settings.readers: A church that had heard of Paul, perhaps with some suspicion (3:8 shows that slanders about him were going around), and that he needs as allies for the west.

settings.to: The Roman believers, Jewish and Gentile
settings.when: At the end of the introduction, before the argument begins
settings.why: To say in two verses what the letter will prove: that the good news reveals God's righteousness to everyone who believes, with Habakkuk 2:4 as the text. Whatever else the letter does (and it does a great deal), it tells why the gospel is not shameful.
settings.readers: A church at the heart of an empire that honored power and success, and could find a crucified Messiah hard to be proud of.

settings.by: Paul, in the style of a Jewish teacher's indictment of the nations
settings.to: Said of "them," the people who suppress the truth; heard by the mixed church in Rome. In 2:1 the "them" becomes "you."
settings.when: As the first stage of the argument that all need the gospel
settings.why: To show that the nations have no defense for their idolatry and its results, in terms that Jewish listeners would accept, so that 2:1 can turn the same charge on anyone who agrees. It is not a full account of Gentile life but an indictment that serves the argument; Paul knows good Gentiles (2:14–15).
settings.readers: Romans who lived among the statues and cults of the capital, and Jews who had learned to see them as idolatry. The passage speaks to both: it reminds the Gentiles of what they left and the Jews of what they condemned.
views: Paul uses a familiar argument (Wisdom of Solomon 13–14) to establish common ground before turning on it.
The passage retells Genesis 1–3 and the golden calf, so that "they" includes Israel (Hooker, Hays, Wright).
It is the portrait of the pagan world that a moralizing hearer applauds, before 2:1 (Stowers).

traditions.q: Can people know God from creation alone? (1:19–20)
views: Yes. The First Vatican Council taught, citing Romans 1:20, that God can be known with certainty by the natural light of human reason from created things, and the Catechism repeats it (CCC 31–36); but saving truth needs revelation (CCC 36–38).

The Orthodox do not use the Western term "natural theology." They teach that God is known in creation by his uncreated energies, though his essence is beyond knowing, and that real knowledge of him comes in the Church and in prayer (as summarized by Kallistos Ware).

All people have some knowledge of God and of his law, but not of his grace. Luther's Heidelberg Disputation (theses 19–20) warns against reading God from creation without the cross; only the gospel shows what God is for us.

Creation leaves everyone without excuse, but sin has so darkened the mind that it cannot lead to saving knowledge (Calvin; Westminster Confession 1.1). Karl Barth went further and denied that natural theology has any place at all, in his "No!" to Emil Brunner (1934). Reformed theologians have been divided over this.

The light of nature and the works of creation show God's goodness, wisdom and power enough to leave people without excuse, but not enough to give the knowledge needed for salvation (Second London Confession 1.1).

traditions.q: Does Romans 1:26–27 condemn all same-sex relationships?
views: Yes. The Catechism teaches that homosexual acts are "intrinsically disordered" and cannot be approved, citing Romans 1:24–27 among others (CCC 2357); it asks that people with such inclinations be received with respect, compassion and sensitivity, and be called to chastity (CCC 2358–2359).
Chrysostom, whom the Orthodox churches honor as a Father and teacher of the Church, read the passage as a condemnation of the acts (Homilies on Romans 4).

Lutherans are divided. The Lutheran Church–Missouri Synod holds that the acts are sin (Commission on Theology and Church Relations, 1981). In 2009 the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America adopted a social statement and voted to allow ministers in committed, lifelong same-gender relationships, reading the Bible's few texts in the light of the gospel and of the lives of those affected.

The Anglican Communion is divided. The Lambeth Conference of 1998 resolved that homosexual practice is incompatible with Scripture (Resolution I.10). The Episcopal Church in the United States authorized same-sex marriage rites at its General Convention of 2015, and several other provinces rejected that step.

Reformed churches differ. The Westminster Larger Catechism (question 139) names sodomy among the sins against the seventh commandment, and the Presbyterian Church in America holds to the Westminster standards. The Presbyterian Church (U.S.A.) changed its Book of Order in 2015 to describe marriage as between two people, traditionally a man and a woman.

United Methodists have been divided for decades. The Book of Discipline long said that "the practice of homosexuality is incompatible with Christian teaching," and in 2024 the General Conference removed that language and the related bans; some congregations have left over the question.
Southern Baptists teach that God's design for marriage is one man and one woman and treat same-sex acts as sin (Baptist Faith and Message, 2000, article 18, and the convention's resolutions).

title: The Judge Who Judges
sum: Paul turns on a listener. Someone who has nodded at the indictment in chapter 1 is told, "You have no defense, whoever you are, you who sit in judgment," because the judge does the same things (2:1–3). God's kindness is meant to lead to repentance, not to be taken as a pass (2:4–5). God will repay everyone for what they have done, Jew first and Greek as well, because "with God there are no favorites" (2:6–11). Having the law is not the same as doing it, and Gentiles who do what the law contains by nature show that its work is written on their hearts (2:12–16).

From 2:17 the "you" is named: someone who calls himself a Jew, relies on the law, boasts in God and teaches others. Paul asks whether he does what he teaches, and says that God's name is insulted among the Gentiles because of such people, as Isaiah 52:5 says (2:17–24). The chapter ends with circumcision: it is worth something if the law is kept, a Gentile who keeps the law will judge the lawbreaker with the letter and circumcision, and a real Jew is one whose circumcision is of the heart, whose praise comes from God (2:25–29).
readings: Read as a charge against Jews

The traditional reading takes 2:1–16 as aimed at the Jew from the start, since only a Jew would judge by God's law, and 2:17–29 as the open charge. Jews have the law and fail to keep it, so they stand with the Gentiles under judgment (Dunn, Moo, Wright).
Read as a charge against the moralizer

Another reading takes the "you" of 2:1–16 as any person who judges others, Jew or Gentile, a fictional partner in a diatribe, and the "Jew" of 2:17–29 as a Gentile or a Jew who is a stock figure (Stowers, Cranfield). On this reading Paul is not criticizing Judaism, but hypocrisy.
Read as a call to Jews to be what the prophets said

A third reading says Paul is standing with the prophets: a circumcised heart was always God's demand (Deuteronomy 10:16; 30:6; Jeremiah 4:4). He does not abolish Jewishness but defines its inner truth, and the Jews who judge are those who have forgotten it (Jewish and Christian readers of the "Paul within Judaism" school).

views.H: The Jewish community in Rome was large, with many synagogues, and had been expelled once under Claudius (Suetonius, Claudius 25.4; Acts 18:2). The charge of "robbing temples" (2:22) may recall a swindle in AD 19 that led to an earlier expulsion (Josephus, Antiquities 18.81–84). Stoic ideas of conscience and natural law, familiar in Rome, stand behind 2:14–15.
views.C: Scholars dispute who is addressed in 2:1 and 2:17, and a few have argued that 2:16 was added (Bultmann); most defend it. The text has two variants a reader of the KJV will notice: the KJV's Behold at 2:17 and the tense of "judges" in 2:16. The long sentence of 2:17–20 does not reach its main clause until 2:21; some scholars think this reflects Paul's way of speaking in dictation, but that is a view, not a finding.
views.L: The chapter is a diatribe: an imagined partner is questioned and answered. The shape is a pair: 2:1–16 on judgment and impartiality, with a chiasm in 2:7–10 (eternal life, anger, trouble, glory), and 2:17–29 on the Jew. The pun on "Jew" and "praise" closes the chapter (2:29).
views.J: God's impartiality, judgment according to deeds, the Gentiles who do what is right, and the heart circumcision of Deuteronomy are all Jewish ideas, and the Mishnah says that "all Israel has a share in the world to come" while still teaching judgment by deeds (Sanhedrin 10:1; Avot 3:15). The question for Jewish readers is whether Paul's picture of a law-boasting Jew fits any real Jewish teacher; most scholars say it is a type.
views.T: Origen and Chrysostom took 2:14 of Gentiles who follow a natural law. The later Augustine, against Pelagius, read it of Gentile Christians in whom the Spirit writes the law. Luther read 2:13 as a standard no one meets without grace. Calvin used 2:14–15 for the natural law that leaves every person without excuse. The churches still disagree about 2:6–11 (see the card) and about the fate of people who never heard the gospel.

deep.h: How the chapter fits with "not by works"
deep.b:
Paul says that God will pay each person back "according to his works" (2:6), that the doers of the law "will be justified" (2:13), and that those who persevere in doing good will get eternal life (2:7). In 3:20 and 3:28 he says that no one is justified by works of the law. Churches and scholars have solved the puzzle in several ways.

Hypothetical: Paul describes the standard no one meets, to show that all need grace (Luther). Real but fulfilled by the Spirit: the final verdict is by works, and believers meet it by the life the Spirit produces (Cranfield, Wright, Dunn). Merit by grace: the good works of the justified are truly rewarded with eternal life because grace makes them so (Council of Trent). Common ground: Paul agrees with the synagogue that God judges by deeds; his news is that the Messiah and the Spirit make obedience possible (Sanders, Donfried). Gentiles: the doers are Gentile Christians. See the card below for the churches' answers.

deep.h: The law written on the heart
deep.b:
2:14–15 has been read in three main ways. Natural law: every person has a sense of right and wrong that corresponds to what the law says, the view of the Greek fathers, Aquinas and Calvin. Christian Gentiles: Paul describes people in whom the Spirit has written the new covenant law of Jeremiah 31:33 (the later Augustine, Barth, Cranfield, Wright). A Jewish idea: the Torah and creation agree, as the philosopher Philo taught.

The first reading underlies Catholic teaching on natural law and parts of the Reformed tradition's teaching on the "civil use" of the law; the second belongs to Barth and Cranfield, who denied that fallen human nature could do what the law requires. See the natural revelation card at 1:19–20.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the "you" is a mirror, then a Jew
deep.b:
One way to hold the readings together is to say that the "you" shifts on purpose. In 2:1–5 it is anyone who agrees with 1:18–32, left unnamed so that each reader supplies himself. By 2:17 Paul has narrowed the "you" to the one reader in the room who has the most to lose from the argument: the Jewish teacher. Paul's own earlier life, as he describes it in Philippians 3:4–6 and Galatians 1:13–14, may be in the picture: a man confident in the law who judged others.

This overlaps with scholars who take 2:1 as universal and 2:17 as Jewish (Cranfield, Fitzmyer), and with Nathan's parable in 2 Samuel 12:1–7. It is a suggestion, not a settled reading.

echoes: Deuteronomy 10:17; Deuteronomy 10:16; Deuteronomy 30:6; Jeremiah 31:33; Jeremiah 4:4; Jeremiah 9:25–26; Psalm 62:12; Proverbs 24:12; Isaiah 52:5; Ezekiel 36:20–27; Exodus 20:14–15; Genesis 29:35; Wisdom of Solomon 11:23; Wisdom of Solomon 12; Matthew 16:27; Acts 10:34; 2 Corinthians 3:3–6

settings.to: An imagined partner who judges others, left unnamed at first: a Gentile moralizer, a Jew, or any reader who has agreed with chapter 1 (views differ). The Roman believers hear the exchange.
settings.when: Straight after the indictment of chapter 1, as the second stage of the argument that all are under sin
settings.why: To remove the escape route of the person who thinks that condemning other people's sin protects him from the same verdict, and to show that God's judgment will be impartial: by deeds, to Jew first and Greek as well. The kindness of God that delays judgment is meant to lead to repentance (2:4).
settings.readers: Roman believers, Jews and Gentiles, who might look down on one another (the weak and the strong of chapters 14–15) and needed to hear that God has no favorites. Many of them knew Jewish teaching on God's impartiality.
views: The partner is a Gentile who agrees with Paul's list of vices and sits in judgment on others (Stowers).
Only a Jew would judge by God's law; the "you" of 2:1 is the same as that of 2:17 (Dunn, Wright, Moo).

settings.what: The charge against the one who calls himself a Jew
settings.to: A person who is "called a Jew," relies on the law, boasts in God and teaches others. Whether he is a typical Jewish teacher, a Gentile who has taken on the name, or a rhetorical figure is debated.
settings.when: After the argument of 2:1–16, as the sharper form of the same charge
settings.why: To say that having the law, circumcision and the name "Jew" does not exempt anyone from the verdict, and that God's name suffers when his people break the law they teach (Isaiah 52:5). It sets up the question about the Jew's advantage (3:1) and the claim that all are under sin (3:9). For Paul's Jewish readers, the cure is inward circumcision, as the prophets said.
settings.readers: Jewish believers in Rome, who knew the tradition that circumcision and the law were Israel's gifts, and Gentile believers, who might be tempted to look down on Jews or to take on Jewish identity themselves.
views: The traditional reading: Paul addresses a typical Jew with a failing teacher's pride.
A Gentile who calls himself a Jew
The partner is a Gentile adopting Jewish identity, a proselyte or would-be proselyte (Stowers; Thorsteinsson).
The sketch is a rhetorical type of hypocrisy and does not describe Jews as a whole (Dunn, Fitzmyer).

traditions.q: Paul says God will repay everyone "according to his works" (2:6, 13), yet that no one is justified by works (3:20). How do the churches fit these together?
views: The justified grow in grace and their good works, done by God's grace, truly merit eternal life as a reward (Council of Trent, session 6, chapter 16 and canon 32). The Catechism says merit is itself a gift of grace (CCC 2006–2011).

Faith alone justifies, and good works necessarily follow as fruit. At the last judgment works will be named as evidence of faith, not as its cause (Augsburg Confession 4 and 6; Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration 4).
Believers will be judged and rewarded, but their works are accepted only because they are in Christ and are the fruit and evidence of faith (Westminster Confession 16.5–6; Calvin on Romans 2).

Justification is by faith alone, by grace, as the root; holiness is its fruit; Wesley taught that believers are judged by their works as proof of a living faith, while denying that they earn their standing (Wesley's sermons and Notes).

Faith and works belong together as parts of one life of salvation; the Orthodox deny that a person is justified by faith alone and affirm that faith works through love (Confession of Dositheus, decree 13).

traditions.q: Can people who never heard the gospel be saved? (2:12–16)
views: Those who through no fault of their own do not know the gospel but seek God and, moved by grace, try to do his will as known through conscience, may be saved; yet all salvation comes through Christ and his Church (Vatican II, Lumen Gentium 16; CCC 847–848).

The elect who cannot be called by preaching may be saved by Christ through the Spirit; but those not professing the Christian religion cannot be saved, however carefully they live by the light of nature (Westminster Confession 10.3–4).

The Second London Confession repeats the Westminster teaching: people who do not profess the Christian religion cannot be saved, however diligently they frame their lives by the light of nature (10.4). Many Baptists today are divided on how this applies.

Article 18 says it is to be rejected that every person shall be saved by the law or sect he professes, if he frames his life by that law and the light of nature, since Scripture sets out only the name of Jesus Christ whereby people must be saved.

Orthodox teachers often sum up the Orthodox position in the saying that we know where the Church is, but we cannot say where it is not. The Church is where salvation is given, and the judgment of those outside is left to God without defining their fate (see Kallistos Ware, The Orthodox Church).

title: All Under Sin, and God's Righteousness Revealed
sum: Paul's imagined Jewish partner asks what is left of Israel's advantage. Much, Paul answers: the Jews were put in charge of the oracles of God, and their unbelief cannot cancel God's faithfulness (3:1–4). Three more objections, one about God's justice and one about doing evil that good may come, are rejected with "By no means!" (3:5–8). The verdict follows: Jews and Greeks alike are "under sin," and a chain of six Scripture passages says so (3:9–18). The law speaks to those inside it to close every mouth, because by works of the law no flesh will be justified (3:19–20).

Then comes "But now" (3:21–26), the center of the letter. Apart from the law, though witnessed by the Law and the Prophets, God's righteousness has been made plain through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe. All sinned and lack God's glory, and they are justified freely, by his grace, through the redemption in Christ Jesus, whom God put forward as the place of atonement by his blood, to show that he is righteous and justifies the one who has faith in Jesus. Boasting is therefore shut out; God is one God of Jews and Gentiles; and faith does not cancel the law but makes it stand (3:27–31).
readings: Read as a courtroom

The Reformation reading hears a law court: God the judge, the sinner guilty, the verdict "righteous" given for Christ's sake and received by faith. "Justify" means declare to be in the right; "redemption" and "atonement" give the price and the sacrifice by which the judge can be both just and the justifier (Luther, Calvin, Moo).
Read as a temple and a family

Catholic and Orthodox readers hear sacrifice and participation: Christ is the new atonement lid, his blood cleanses, and justification is a being made righteous by sharing in his life (Council of Trent; Orthodox teaching on theosis). Faith is the beginning of a transformation, not only a verdict.
Read as the story of God's covenant

The New Perspective hears Israel's story: God's righteousness is his faithfulness to the promise to Abraham; "works of the law" are the badges that kept Jews and Gentiles apart; "justification" declares who belongs to the family of God (Dunn, Wright, Hays). The courtroom and the temple are inside that story.

views.H: The picture of the "place of atonement" draws on the temple's Day of Atonement, kept by Jews as a day of fasting (Philo, Special Laws 2.193–203), a Jewish fast that Roman writers also knew (Suetonius, Augustus 76). The word "redemption" recalls the slave market, where a person might be bought and freed, and the Exodus. The "works of the law" of 3:20 and 3:28 may be the practices that marked Jews off in the city: circumcision, Sabbath and food laws, which Roman authors noticed (Tacitus, Histories 5.5).
views.C: Scholars debate the source of 3:24–26, many hearing a pre-Pauline formula behind the language of "redemption," "blood" and "passing over" (Bultmann, Käsemann, and others), and the faith of 3:22 and 3:26 (Christ's faithfulness or faith in Christ?). The Byzantine text adds "and upon all" at 3:22; the KJV's "therefore we conclude" at 3:28 reflects a variant. The chain of quotations in 3:10–18 is Paul's own gathering of Psalms and Isaiah.
views.L: The chapter is the hinge of the letter: the long indictment (1:18–3:20) closes with "every mouth" shut, and "But now" (3:21) opens the second movement. The diatribe style, with its objections and "By no means!", continues in 3:1–8 and 3:27–31. 3:21–26 is one sentence in Greek, built round the contrasts of law and faith, revealed and hidden, passing over and showing. The "righteous" family of words occurs seven times in the six verses of 3:21–26.
views.J: "The Jew's advantage" (3:1–2) is affirmed, not removed. "Oracles of God" names Israel's Scripture. The chain of Psalms and Isaiah turns Israel's own prayers into accusations of all humanity, which Jewish readers may note is a rereading of texts about the wicked among Israel and her enemies. The Day of Atonement and the sacrifices stand behind 3:25. Jewish scholars (Levine, Fredriksen, Boyarin) differ on whether Paul's "apart from the law" abolishes Torah for Jews or only for Gentiles; 3:31 is cited on both sides.
views.T: Chrysostom and Origen read 3:21–26 as the great work of God's love; Augustine, as grace that gives the faith it asks; Aquinas, as an infusion of righteousness. Luther called 3:23–26 the chief point and central place of the letter and of the whole Bible, and in his German translation added "alone" at 3:28. The Council of Trent responded, and the 1999 Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification (Lutheran World Federation and the Catholic Church) tried to bring the two sides together, with reservations on both. Wesley's Aldersgate experience came while he heard Luther's preface to Romans read aloud (24 May 1738).

deep.b:
"But now." A turn in time: what was hidden has now been made plain (3:21; 3:26 "the present time"). "Apart from the law." God's righteousness is not earned by keeping the commandments, yet "the Law and the Prophets give witness to it": Genesis 15, Psalm 32, Habakkuk 2:4, Isaiah 53. "Through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe": Jew and Gentile alike, with "no distinction" (the grammar is debated; see the note). "All sinned and lack the glory": the reason no distinction is needed. "Justified freely, by his grace": a gift. "The redemption in Christ Jesus": a release at a cost. "The place of atonement ... by his blood": the sacrifice. "To show his righteousness": God's own righteousness is at stake, as it was in 3:3–5. "Because in his forbearance God had passed over sins done earlier": God's patience looked like injustice. "That he himself would be righteous and would justify": the paradox solved in the cross.

Every phrase has been read differently by different churches. The notes give the readings and the card sets out the positions. The Plain English Translation does not choose among them except where the Greek forces a choice.

The phrase occurs in 3:20 and 3:28, and in Galatians 2:16 and 3. Until the second half of the twentieth century most Protestants read it as meaning any deeds done to earn God's favor, and Paul's argument as the rejection of Jewish legalism. In 1977 E. P. Sanders published Paul and Palestinian Judaism, arguing that Judaism of the time taught that Israel was chosen by grace and that obedience was the response, and that it was not a religion of earning salvation. Many scholars have accepted Sanders' picture, and it has led them to ask again what Paul's objection was; others (Gathercole, Carson) think some Jewish texts expected vindication on the basis of obedience.

James Dunn, N. T. Wright and others (the "New Perspective") say the phrase refers to the laws that marked the Jew off from the Gentile: circumcision, Sabbath, food laws. Paul's objection is that these cannot be the limit of God's people. Others (Moo, Schreiner and the Reformed tradition) reply that the phrase means the whole law, and that Paul's point is that no one can do it. The Dead Sea text 4QMMT, "Some of the Works of the Torah," uses the Hebrew phrase for specific rules a group required, which supports the first view; but its rules are also demands of the whole Torah, which supports the second. Some scholars hold that the phrase names the whole law as it functioned to separate Jews from Gentiles. The Plain English Translation keeps the literal "works of the law" and the notes give the options.

deep.h: Faith in Christ or Christ's faithfulness?
deep.b:
The Greek pistis Iesou Christou (3:22; also 3:26; Galatians 2:16, 3:22; Philippians 3:9) can be read either way. The objective reading (faith in Christ) is the traditional one and appears in most translations. It makes good sense of Paul's insistence that people are justified by believing (3:22 "for all who believe"), and he writes "believe in Christ" with a different construction in Galatians 2:16. The subjective reading (the faithfulness of Christ) was argued by Richard Hays (1983) and since by Douglas Campbell and others. It says that the plain meaning of "X's faith" is the faith that X has, that "through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe" is otherwise repetitive, and that Paul's gospel is about what Christ did, in obedience (5:19), not first about what people do.

Both sides say the other makes the sentence redundant or strained. The Plain English Translation uses "faith in Jesus Christ," the reading of most translations and of Cranfield, Dunn, Fitzmyer and Moo, and notes the other in the gloss.

deep.title: Claude's theory: a thread of glory from 1:21 to 8:30
deep.b:
The word "glory" (doxa) runs through Romans as a story. People refused to glorify God (1:21) and swapped his glory for images (1:23). All "lack the glory of God" (3:23). Abraham, by contrast, "gave glory to God" (4:20). Believers boast in the hope of the glory of God (5:2), will be glorified with Christ (8:17), and are those whom God finally glorifies (8:30). Creation itself waits for the freedom of the glory of God's children (8:21).

If so, 3:23 is neither a stray remark nor a sentence about guilt only: it states the condition of a creature made for glory who lacks it, and the whole letter tells how it is restored. The reading overlaps with Jewish traditions about Adam's lost glory (1QS 4:23), with James Dunn's reading of 3:23, and with N. T. Wright's emphasis on the image of God. The thread is clearest in the Greek; the Plain English Translation renders the verb of 1:21 as "praise" and the noun as "glory," so a reader of the Plain English Translation should check the notes.

settings.what: The Jew's advantage and four objections
settings.by: Paul, with an imagined Jewish partner
settings.to: The partner who asks, "What is the advantage of the Jew?" and objects that Paul's teaching would make God unfaithful or unjust; heard by the Roman believers
settings.when: Straight after the charge of 2:17–29, as the first step of the argument that Jews also are under sin
settings.why: To affirm Israel's real privilege, the oracles of God (3:2), and to show that Israel's unfaithfulness cannot undo God's faithfulness. It meets in advance the charge that Paul teaches "let us do evil so that good may come," a slander that he knew was circulating (3:8).
settings.readers: Probably Jewish Christians in Rome who wondered whether Paul had written off the Jews (this is a reconstruction), and Gentile Christians who might take the answer for granted. 3:3 is the first form of the question that chapters 9–11 will answer.

settings.what: The charge that all are under sin, and the chain of Scripture
settings.to: Jews and Gentiles, since Paul has "already charged" both (3:9); the chain of Psalms and Isaiah speaks to "those inside the law" and closes every mouth
settings.when: The conclusion of the indictment that began at 1:18
settings.why: To state the verdict: no one is righteous, and the law, far from rescuing, shows sin and closes every mouth. The chain of quotations turns Israel's own Scripture into evidence, so that Jews cannot say the charge is only about Gentiles.
settings.readers: A church of Jews and Gentiles who had each been tempted to see themselves as better than the other (14:1–15:13). It deflated both.

settings.what: God's righteousness made plain through Christ
settings.to: The Roman believers: Jewish Christians who knew the temple and the Day of Atonement and Gentile Christians who knew the slave market and the courts
settings.when: The turn of the letter, after the indictment and before the example of Abraham
settings.why: To say what God has done in Christ so that sinners may be justified without God's justice being dropped. It uses pictures from the law court (justify), the slave market (redemption) and the temple (place of atonement) to speak to a mixed audience. For Jewish believers it shows how the cross fits the sacrifices; for Gentile believers it shows how Israel's Scripture stands behind the gospel.
settings.readers: Believers who needed a ground for their unity in Christ, other than the law that divided them.
views: God declares the sinner righteous on the basis of Christ's death (Luther, Calvin, Moo).
Christ is the atonement lid where God and humanity meet, and the sacrifice by which sin is cleansed (Manson, Wright; Orthodox and Catholic tradition).
God keeps his promise to Abraham by dealing with sin and opening the covenant to all (Dunn, Wright, Hays).

settings.what: Boasting excluded; one God of Jews and Gentiles
settings.to: The imagined partner and the Roman believers
settings.why: To show what follows: no one can boast of earning God's favor, nor can Jews claim a monopoly on God, since he is one. It answers the objection of 3:31 that faith cancels the law by saying it makes the law stand, a claim chapter 4 proves from Abraham.
settings.readers: Jewish and Gentile believers who needed one God and one faith in place of two classes.

traditions.q: What does "justified" mean, and how do faith and works relate? (3:21–31)
views: Justification is not only the forgiveness of sins but the sanctification and renewal of the inner person by God's grace, received first in baptism, and increased through faith working in love and cooperation with grace. Faith is necessary but not alone (Council of Trent, session 6; CCC 1987–1995).

The Fathers speak of salvation as healing and sharing in God's life (theosis) more than as a legal verdict. Faith and works are two sides of one life, and justification is not separated from sanctification. Orthodox churches took no part in the Western debates of the 1500s; when Reformation teaching reached the East in the Confession attributed to Cyril Lucaris (1629), the Synod of Jerusalem answered it in the Confession of Dositheus (1672), which denies justification by faith alone.

God declares sinners righteous for Christ's sake, by faith alone, apart from works. Good works follow as fruit (Augsburg Confession 4 and 6). Luther made this the chief article, and later Lutherans summed it up in the formula that it is the article by which the church stands or falls (Smalcald Articles II.1). In the 1999 Joint Declaration the Lutheran World Federation and the Catholic Church agreed that their remaining differences do not warrant mutual condemnation; some Lutheran theologians disagree.

God pardons sinners and accepts them as righteous, not by infusing righteousness but by crediting to them Christ's obedience and satisfaction, received by faith alone (Westminster Confession 11.1; Calvin, Institutes 3.11).

Justification is God's pardon, by faith alone; sanctification is the work of God in the believer that follows, and both are free grace (Wesley, Sermons on Salvation by Faith and Justification by Faith). In 2006 the World Methodist Council associated itself with the Joint Declaration.

God justifies by imputing the obedience of Christ, with faith as the instrument (Second London Confession 11); justification is "God's gracious and full acquittal ... of all sinners who repent and believe in Christ" (Baptist Faith and Message, 2000, article 4).

"We are accounted righteous before God, only for the merit of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, by faith" (Article 11); good works are the fruit of faith (Article 12). Anglicans include Evangelicals, who stress the forensic reading, and Anglo-Catholics, who stress the sacraments and the process of growth.

Pentecostal churches teach justification by grace through faith (Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths) and add that a believer is to expect new life in the Spirit; Oneness Pentecostals teach that baptism in Jesus' name and the gift of the Spirit belong with faith in salvation (United Pentecostal Church).

Christ's whole life and death were a free offering of love to the Father, a sacrifice that gives redemption and reparation, atonement and satisfaction (CCC 615–618; Aquinas, Summa III q.48, on merit, satisfaction, sacrifice, redemption and efficiency; Anselm's Why God Became Man).

Christ defeats death and the devil, heals human nature by uniting it with God, and recapitulates Adam (Irenaeus, Athanasius). The Easter hymn sings that Christ is risen, "trampling down death by death." Many Orthodox teachers regard the Western language of penal satisfaction as foreign to the Fathers.

Luther taught Christ's victory over sin, death and the devil (the "classic" view, as Gustaf Aulén argued) and the "joyful exchange" in which Christ takes our sin and gives his righteousness; Lutheran orthodoxy taught vicarious satisfaction (Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration 3).

Christ bore the penalty for sin in the place of those he saves, satisfying God's justice (penal substitution; Calvin, Institutes 2.16; Westminster Confession 8.5). The Canons of Dort teach that his death is sufficient for all but efficient for the elect.
Christ made on the cross "a full, perfect, and sufficient sacrifice, oblation, and satisfaction, for the sins of the whole world" (1662 Communion service; Articles 2 and 31).

Christ's death is "a perfect redemption, propitiation, and satisfaction for all the sins of the whole world" (Methodist Articles, Article 20); Wesley held the atonement is for all, against the Calvinists.

Anabaptist and Mennonite teaching speaks of Christ's death as the offering of the Lamb and victory over evil without laying down a single theory (Confession of Faith in a Mennonite Perspective, 1995). Some Mennonite theologians (J. Denny Weaver) argue for the "Christus Victor" view against penal substitution as a source of violence; others defend substitution.

title: Abraham, Father of All Who Believe
sum: Paul now proves from Scripture that the way of faith is not new. What did Abraham, "our forefather according to the flesh," find? If he was justified by works he could boast, but Genesis 15:6 says he believed God and it was reckoned to him as righteousness. A worker's wages are a debt, but God "justifies the ungodly," and David's Psalm 32 blesses the person whose sin the Lord does not reckon (4:1–8). The timing settles it: Abraham was reckoned righteous before he was circumcised, so he is father of all who believe without circumcision, and of the circumcised who follow his faith (4:9–12).

The promise that he would inherit the world did not come through the law, which only produces anger, but through the righteousness of faith, so that it depends on grace and is certain for all his offspring, Jew and Gentile (4:13–17). Abraham believed against hope in the God who makes the dead alive and calls the things that are not as though they were; he looked at his dead body and Sarah's dead womb, and his faith did not grow weak (4:17–22). The words were written for us too: we believe in the One who raised Jesus from the dead, who was handed over for our trespasses and raised for our justification (4:23–25).
readings: Read as an argument from Scripture

Paul argues in the way a Jewish teacher would, from the order of the Genesis story (15, then 17) and from a word shared by two texts ("reckon" in Genesis 15:6 and Psalm 32:2). The conclusion is that faith, not circumcision or works, was the ground of Abraham's standing.
Read as an answer to the Jewish tradition of Abraham

Many Jews read Abraham as the model of faithful obedience under testing (Sirach 44 and 1 Maccabees 2:52, which are Scripture for Catholic and Orthodox Christians; Jubilees, which is Scripture only for the Ethiopian Orthodox church). Paul answers that Genesis 15:6 comes before the testing and before the law, so it cannot be the reward of obedience (Dunn, Gathercole).
Read as the founding of one family

A third reading emphasizes the family: Abraham is the father of Jews and Gentiles who share his trust, so Gentiles need not become Jews to belong, and Jews need not give up their identity to share the promise (Wright, Fredriksen, Nanos). The chapter is then less about how an individual is saved than about who belongs to the people of God.

views.H: Abraham was the most honored ancestor in the Jewish world and a figure the Roman believers knew. The language of accounts ("reckon," "wages," "debt") belongs to the Roman economy of work and favors. Circumcision was a mark Roman writers noticed and mocked. The "father of many nations" had a particular edge in a city whose Gentile believers asked whether they belonged to the Jewish story.
views.C: The text has two significant variants: the word "found" in 4:1 (three readings) and the "not" before "considered" in 4:19. Many scholars hear an earlier source or creed in 4:24–25. The question of the relation between Paul and James 2:14–26 runs through the chapter, as does the question of whether 4:1 asks "What did Abraham find?" or "What shall we say about Abraham?"
views.L: The chapter is a midrash on Genesis 15–17, in order: the verse (4:3), the gloss with Psalm 32 (4:6–8), the circumcision of Genesis 17 (4:9–12), the promise (4:13–17), and Abraham's faith when he was old (4:18–22). The word "reckon" (logizomai) occurs eleven times. The closing verses (4:23–25) turn the story to the present with "for us too." Abraham's "giving glory" in 4:20 answers the failure to give glory in 1:21.
views.J: Abraham in Jewish tradition is both the first monotheist and the model of obedience. Paul's reading of Genesis 15:6 differs from the common one that links it with the testing of Genesis 22 (Sirach 44:20; 1 Maccabees 2:52), but it is an argument within Judaism about what Genesis means. Jewish readers note that the rabbis also discussed whether converts can call Abraham "our father" (Mishnah Bikkurim 1:4). The promise to Abraham that his seed will be many is for Jews a promise about Israel; Paul extends it. Whether he thereby takes it away is the question of 9–11 and of the "Paul within Judaism" debate.
views.T: Justification by faith in Abraham's case became the central text of the Reformation. Luther called Romans 4 the proof that faith alone saves. Calvin used the verb "reckon" for imputation. Catholic teaching (Trent) read Abraham's faith as the start of a justice that grows by works. James 2:21–24 became the counter-text, and the early church (Augustine, Chrysostom) read the two letters together. Reformed teaching on the covenant sign draws on 4:11 for the case that baptism replaces circumcision, which Baptists reject.

deep.h: Abraham in Jewish tradition, and Paul's reply
deep.b:
When Paul asks what Abraham "found," his Roman readers would have heard a standard answer: Abraham found favor with God by his obedience. Sirach (Scripture for Catholic and Orthodox Christians) praises Abraham, who kept the law of the Most High and was found faithful when tested (Sirach 44:19–21). First Maccabees (likewise), in the dying Mattathias' speech, asks whether Abraham was not found faithful in testing, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness (1 Maccabees 2:52). Jubilees 23:10 (Scripture only for the Ethiopian Orthodox church) praises him as perfect in righteousness. The Mishnah says he kept the whole Torah before it was given (Qiddushin 4:14). The Dead Sea letter 4QMMT ends by saying that doing what it urges will be reckoned to the reader as righteousness, in words close to Genesis 15:6 and Psalm 106:31.

In this tradition, "reckoned as righteousness" is the reward for faithfulness. Paul reads the verse in its place in Genesis: it is said in Genesis 15, before the tests (Genesis 22) and before circumcision (Genesis 17), when Abraham has done nothing but believe a promise about a child. The shift is from reward to gift. Readers of every tradition note the point; they differ on whether Paul's reading overturns the Jewish one or answers a narrow form of it (Dunn, Sanders, Gathercole, Barclay).

The Greek word logizomai means to count something to someone's account. In the Reformation, "imputation" became the name for the teaching that God credits Christ's righteousness to the believer. The Reformers saw it in 4:3–8, 22–24, where righteousness is "reckoned" without works. The Catholic response (Trent) is that the verse describes a righteousness that God gives and that is really in the person. The New Perspective says what is reckoned is the status of a member of the covenant family (Wright). Paul never says "Christ's righteousness is reckoned to us"; the chapter says that faith is reckoned as righteousness. The churches' positions are on the card at 3:21–31.

deep.title: Claude's theory: Paul reads Genesis in a zigzag
deep.b:
Chapter 4 follows the Abraham story in a pattern. It starts with Genesis 15:6 (4:3), moves to David and Psalm 32 (4:6–8), jumps ahead to the circumcision of Genesis 17 (4:9–12), returns with the promise of the "world" and the nations in Genesis 17:5 (4:13–17), goes back to Genesis 15:5, "So will your offspring be" (4:18), and then to the old-age scene of Genesis 17:17 and 18 (4:19). The zigzag between Genesis 15 and 17 is not accidental: each time Paul uses the later chapter to answer a question that the earlier one raises (is faith enough? does circumcision matter? who are the nations?).

This reading is mine; commentators note the sequence of Genesis 15 and 17 in Romans 4 but I know of none who sets it out as a deliberate zigzag. The argument depends on the Greek order of the quotations and so cannot be seen in the Plain English Translation unless the reader keeps the Genesis references at hand.

echoes: Genesis 15:1–6; Genesis 17:5; Genesis 17:10–14; Genesis 17:17; Genesis 18:12; Psalm 32:1–2; Psalm 106:31; Exodus 23:7; Proverbs 17:15; Isaiah 53:12; 2 Maccabees 7:28; Sirach 44:19–21; 1 Maccabees 2:52; Jubilees 23:10; James 2:21–24; Galatians 3:6–18; Hebrews 11:8–19

settings.what: Abraham justified by faith, not works
settings.by: Paul, with the diatribe's question "What are we to say?"
settings.to: The Roman believers, Jewish and Gentile; the imagined partner who holds that Abraham earned his standing
settings.when: After 3:27–31, as the proof from Scripture that the way of faith is the oldest way
settings.why: To show from Genesis and the Psalms that God has always justified by faith, not by works, and that even the great sinner David lived by God's refusal to count his sin. It answers the objection that faith cancels the law (3:31).
settings.readers: Jewish Christians who honored Abraham as the model of obedience, and Gentile Christians who needed to hear that they could claim him as father without becoming Jews.

settings.to: Jewish and Gentile believers in Rome
settings.when: After the proof from Genesis 15:6 and Psalm 32
settings.why: To say that Abraham's faith was reckoned before he was circumcised, so that circumcision is a seal of a righteousness already given. It makes Abraham father of believing Gentiles and of believing Jews. For Jewish law, it speaks to circumcision as God's command to Abraham and his house, and says it is not the way a non-Jew comes to be in the family.
settings.readers: Gentile believers who were tempted to be circumcised to be safe, and Jewish believers who wondered about their status.

settings.what: The promise by faith, the father of us all
settings.when: The center of the chapter, with Genesis 17:5 as the text
settings.why: To say the promise rests on faith, not law, so that it may be by grace and certain for all of Abraham's offspring, those who belong to the law and those who share his faith. It deals with the fear that the Gentile inclusion put the promise at risk.
settings.readers: A mixed church, in which both groups needed to hear that they belonged to the same family.

settings.what: Abraham's faith in the God who raises the dead, and ours
settings.when: The end of the argument of 3:21–4:25
settings.why: To describe the faith that justifies: trust in the God who gives life to the dead, Abraham's in a child, ours in the raising of Jesus. It connects the Genesis story with the confession of the resurrection (4:24–25), and prepares for the peace and hope of chapter 5.
settings.readers: Believers who were asked to trust in a crucified and risen Messiah as Abraham trusted in a promise.

traditions.q: Does baptism take the place of circumcision? (4:11)
views: Yes. Baptism, like circumcision, is a sign and seal of the covenant of grace, and so the infants of believers are to be baptized as the sons of Abraham were circumcised (Calvin, Institutes 4.16; Westminster Confession 28.1, 4).
No. Baptists answer that circumcision belonged to the Abrahamic covenant with his physical offspring, while baptism is for those who profess repentance and faith (Second London Confession 29.2).

Circumcision foreshadowed baptism and prepared for it by teaching faith in the coming Christ; baptism, which does what circumcision pointed to, is given to infants as well as adults (Aquinas, Summa III q.70, a.1; Colossians 2:11–12).

Baptism follows personal faith, and the covenant sign is no longer one of birth. Early Anabaptists rejected the argument from circumcision (Schleitheim Confession, article 1, on baptism for those who have learned repentance), and Calvin used the argument from circumcision in reply to them (Institutes 4.16).

traditions.q: Paul says Abraham was justified by faith (4:2–3); James says he was justified by works (James 2:21–24). Are these the same teaching?
views: Faith is necessary but must be formed by love and show itself in works; James and Paul speak of different stages of one justification (Council of Trent, session 6, chapters 7 and 10, and canon 9; CCC 1815).

Faith alone justifies, but faith is never alone: where it is real it produces works (Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration 4). Luther found James hard to reconcile with Paul and wrote of it harshly in 1522.

Faith alone justifies, but "it is not alone in the person justified, but is ever accompanied with all other saving graces" (Westminster Confession 11.2); James speaks of the justification of faith's claim before people.
Wesley taught that faith is the only condition of justification and that faith works by love, so that holiness and good works follow; James is read as a warning against a faith without works.
A person is not justified by faith alone but by faith that works through love, "through faith and works" (Confession of Dositheus, decree 13), and James is read with Paul as one teaching.
